title: Teaching
text:
I teach the politics of the criminal legal system as a subject students can analyze rigorously and connect directly to their own communities. My signature course, The Politics of Police and Prisons in the U.S., is the only course on the criminal justice system in Michigan’s Political Science department, and it regularly fills to capacity with a waitlist. In 2025 I rebuilt the course around specifications grading, replacing letter grades with a mastery-based rubric that lets students revise and resubmit their work until it meets a clear standard. I adopted this model to shift students’ attention from chasing points toward genuinely mastering concepts, to reward intellectual risk-taking, and to prepare students for professional settings where work is judged against standards rather than scored.
I design my courses to move students from abstract analysis to direct engagement with political institutions. In Police and Prisons, students build a semester-long portfolio of projects, including concept maps and an Institutional Power Map that asks them to apply what they learn about courts, police, and prisons to the governance of their own hometowns. I bring practitioners and scholars into the classroom — among them a county sheriff, a former public defender, and faculty from allied fields — so that students see how the system operates in practice.
Beyond the classroom, I founded and direct the Violence and Policing Lab, which brings graduate and undergraduate researchers together around the PKAP dataset. Lab members contribute to coding and analyzing the data and, in return, receive sustained mentorship on their own research. We meet bi-weekly for students to present dissertation chapters and independent projects and to receive feedback from me and their peers. The lab creates a structured intellectual community that bridges research training and mentorship, and it has become central to how I support the next generation of scholars.

title: Shea Streeter

Assistant Professor of Political Science · University of Michigan


I study why some acts of state violence become public movements — and why many others never do.

Read the research

title: Shea Streeter
text:
About
I am a political scientist who studies race, police violence, and the politics of accountability in the United States. My research asks why some police killings ignite protest and demands for justice while others pass in silence. I argue that the answer begins with families and their efforts to make claims on the state after their loved one has been killed. The decisions that grieving families make in the aftermath of a killing — whether to mourn privately or to demand justice publicly — determine when private loss becomes a public movement. This reframing changes how we understand the Black Lives Matter movement and the movement for police accountability, revealing that campaigns for justice and reform have been carried, in large part, on the labor of grieving relatives.
My book project, Claiming Justice: Families and the Movement for Police Accountability, develops and tests this argument. I draw on the Police Killings and Protest (PKAP) dataset, an original resource that documents more than 2,000 police killings and codes each for whether it produced protest. I pair that quantitative evidence with interviews and fieldwork among the families of people killed by police, a population that existing research has rarely reached. Together, these sources let me build a three-part theory of grievance, bandwidth, and broadcast that explains how a single death can become a national cause. I direct the Violence and Policing Lab at Michigan, where a team of graduate and undergraduate researchers helps build and analyze this evidence.
My earlier and ongoing work examines state violence and its political consequences from several angles. In the Journal of Politics, I showed that police kill Black and White Americans under strikingly similar circumstances, which points to African Americans’ more frequent contact with police, rather than differences in the encounters themselves, as the most likely source of the threefold racial disparity in police killings. In Public Opinion Quarterly, my coauthor and I demonstrated that Americans’ judgments about police violence turn on whether they perceive the victim as deserving. In a working paper on the 2020 uprising, my collaborator and I find that a county’s prior protest experience, not its rate of police violence, best predicts whether residents mobilized after George Floyd’s murder. Across these projects, I trace how communities translate — or fail to translate — violence into political action.

title: Research
text: My research explains how communities respond to state violence, and why those responses so often diverge. I combine an original dataset of police killings with interviews, fieldwork, and survey experiments to trace the path from a single death to collective political action. The work spans three strands: a book project on families and the demand for accountability, a set of published articles on racial disparities and public opinion in policing, and ongoing studies of the geography and dynamics of protest.

title: Research
text:
Book project

Claiming Justice: Families and the Movement for Police Accountability In progress
This book explains why some police killings lead to protest while others do not by placing families at the center of the story. I argue that the decisions families make in the wake of police violence — whether to grieve privately or demand justice publicly — determine in part when personal loss becomes political mobilization. Drawing on the Police Killings and Protest (PKAP) dataset, interviews, and fieldwork, I develop and test a three-part theory of grievance, bandwidth, and broadcast. The project reveals that movements for police accountability have largely been borne on the efforts of grieving families, reshaping how we understand the Black Lives Matter movement and related mobilizations.

title: Research
text:
Peer-reviewed articles

Police Abuse or Just Deserts? Deservingness Perceptions and State Violence
Shea Streeter and Mackenzie Israel-Trummel Public Opinion Quarterly 86, no. S1 (June 2022): 499–522.
Why do Americans demand justice after some acts of police violence but not others? In a survey experiment that randomizes the race and gender of a victim, we find that support for compensating the victim tracks perceived deservingness: it is highest for a White woman and lowest for a Black woman, and Black respondents are 58 percent more likely than White respondents to favor restitution. Whether the public treats state violence as an injustice to be remedied is bound up with race — a dynamic that helps explain why outwardly similar killings provoke such different demands for accountability.


Abstract



Divergent public responses to police brutality incidents demonstrate that for some, police violence is an injustice that demands remediation, while for others state violence is justice served. We develop a novel survey experiment in which we randomize the race and gender of a victim of police violence, and then provide respondents with an opportunity to establish justice via compensation. We uncover small but consistent effects that financial restitution is most supported for a White female detainee and least supported for a Black female detainee, and this is largely driven by White respondents. Beyond the treatment effects, we show that Black respondents are much more likely to perceive detainees as deserving of restitution; across all treatments, Black respondents are 58 percent more likely than Whites to support a financial settlement. We further show that White respondents’ perceptions of deservingness are highly related to their perceptions of who is at fault for the beating—the detainee or the police—and whether the detainee was involved in crime. Black respondents remain likely to award a settlement even if they think the detainee was at fault and involved in crime. Our results provide further evidence that perceptions of who deserves restorative justice for state violence are entangled with race in targeted ways.

Bringing Abolition In: Addressing Carceral Logics in Social Science Research
Jordie Davies, Jenn Jackson, and Shea Streeter Social Science Quarterly (August 2021).
Social science can unintentionally reproduce the carceral logics it studies, treating police and prisons as fixed features of social life. Drawing on Black feminist and abolitionist thought, we argue that taking abolition seriously as an analytic commitment reframes how scholars ask questions about crime, punishment, and the state, and we press researchers to examine how their own methods and institutions sustain carceral power. The essay grounds a broader commitment in my work: to study state violence on terms that center the people it harms rather than the systems that produce it.


Abstract



Objective. In this essay, we review and offer theoretical groundings and empirical approaches to the study of abolition.


Methods. We begin by demonstrating the ways police and prisons have been used to exploit and dominate marginalized people and argue that abolition offers a path to finding solutions to public safety and racial justice. We draw from black feminist and abolitionist political thought to show how abolition makes space to upend systems of power and domination and develop systems that address the root causes of violence.


Results. We assert that abolitionist research will not only focus on activists’ calls for dismantling the police but will also recognize and engage with activists’ proposals for reimagining public safety. We suggest that social scientists who study abolition, American uprisings, and policing must understand the differences between transformative changes based in abolitionist frameworks versus those that center mass incarceration as a societal given and, ultimately, further reproduce the status quo.


Conclusion. We conclude by suggesting that social scientists must question how researcher practices and universities uphold carceral logics and entrenched hierarchies, determining that abolitionist study will meaningfully engage with the distribution of power.

Lethal Force in Black and White: Assessing Racial Disparities in the Circumstances of Police Killings
Shea Streeter The Journal of Politics 81, no. 3 (July 2019): 1124–1132.
African Americans are nearly three times as likely as White Americans to be killed by police. I ask whether that disparity reflects racial differences in the circumstances of the killings themselves. Applying machine learning to 126 hand-coded variables for 700 police killings from 2015, drawn from the Police Killings and Protest (PKAP) dataset, I find that the decedent’s characteristics, alleged criminal activity, threat level, police actions, and the setting of the encounter do not predict race: the best model classifies race correctly 69 percent of the time, barely above the 66 percent achieved by labeling every decedent White. Once contact occurs, police kill Black and White Americans under largely similar circumstances. The disparity therefore most likely originates in how often African Americans come into contact with police, rather than in what happens during the encounter or in officers’ decisions to shoot. Because only 11 percent of these killings began with a traffic or pedestrian stop, explaining that disproportionate contact requires looking well beyond discretionary stops.


Abstract



African Americans are nearly three times as likely to be killed by police as whites. This paper examines whether this racial disparity is due in part to racial differences in the circumstances of police killings. To assess whether and how these circumstances predict the race of a decedent, I use machine learning techniques and a novel data set of police killings containing over 120 descriptors. I find that decedent characteristics, criminal activity, threat levels, police actions, and the setting of the lethal interaction are not predictive of race, indicating that the police—given contact—are killing blacks and whites under largely similar circumstances. The findings suggest that the racial disparity in the rate of lethal force is most likely driven by higher rates of police contact among African Americans rather than racial differences in the circumstances of the interaction and officer bias in the application of lethal force.

title: Research
text:
Working papers & works in progress

Mobilization Readiness and the Geography of Protest in the 2020 Uprising Working paper
Shea Streeter and Arica Schuett Presented at the 2026 American Political Science Association Conference.
Why did some U.S. counties mobilize during the 2020 racial-justice uprising while others did not? Merging the Crowd Counting Consortium’s record of more than 10,000 protests with county-level data across all 3,100 U.S. counties, we introduce the concept of mobilization readiness — a community’s prior experience with collective action. We find that earlier left-leaning protest activity strongly predicted Floyd-era demonstrations, while local rates of police killings did not.
